A.explanation: Uses $T\cos 40^\circ$ for the vertical component, which is the component for $50^\circ$ to the horizontal. This gives about $3.4\ \text{N}$.

B.explanation: Balances clockwise moment of the $5.2\ \text{N}$ weight at the centre with anticlockwise moment of $T\sin 40^\circ$ at $30\ \text{cm}$, giving $T$ about $4.0\ \text{N}$.

C.explanation: Gives $5.2/\cos 40^\circ$. This places the weight at the end of the rod instead of the centre and uses the wrong trigonometric component.

D.explanation: Gives $5.2/\sin 40^\circ$. This correctly uses $T\sin 40^\circ$ but places the $5.2\ \text{N}$ weight at $30\ \text{cm}$ instead of $15\ \text{cm}$.

hints: Notice the rod is uniform, so its $5.2\ \text{N}$ weight acts at its centre, $15\ \text{cm}$ from the hinge, not at the wire end.
Only the vertical part of the wire tension, $T\sin 40^\circ$, provides an anticlockwise moment about the hinge because the rod is horizontal.
Take moments about the hinge so the unknown hinge force has zero moment, then equate $T\sin 40^\circ \times 30\ \text{cm}$ to $5.2\ \text{N} \times 15\ \text{cm}$.
walkthrough: Take moments about the hinge. This removes the hinge force because its distance from the hinge is zero.
The uniform rod weight $W = 5.2\ \text{N}$ acts downwards at the centre, $0.15\ \text{m}$ from the hinge. Its clockwise moment is $W \times 0.15 = 5.2 \times 0.15 = 0.78\ \text{N m}$.

The tension $T$ in the wire acts at $40^\circ$ to the horizontal at the far end, $0.30\ \text{m}$ from the hinge. Its vertical component is $T\sin 40^\circ$ and its perpendicular distance gives anticlockwise moment $T\sin 40^\circ \times 0.30$.
For equilibrium, sum of moments about hinge is zero: $T\sin 40^\circ \times 0.30 = 0.78$.
